hook: The embedding model is a **10-year mortgage** on your data. Choose with the exit cost in mind.

scenes.title: Quality, cost, language — **in that order for you**
scenes.sub: And validate on YOUR corpus, not the leaderboard
scenes.narration: Three axes for embedding models. Quality: does it rank YOUR document pairs correctly — measure with a small set of known query-answer pairs from your domain. Cost: OpenAI's small model is famously cheap; self-hosted models trade API cost for GPU cost. Language support: English-only models quietly fail on Hindi text — for your corpus, multilingual support isn't a nice-to-have. The procedure is identical to GA-02's model selection: build a small relevance eval set, run candidates, pick the cheapest that passes. The leaderboard is a starting shortlist, never the decision.

items.s: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark — a shortlist, not a verdict
query → the doc that MUST rank #1 → measure hit@5 per candidate
OpenAI/Cohere/Voyage APIs: zero ops. sentence-transformers: private, GPU-billed

scenes.narration: The selection workflow. Shortlist from MTEB — the public benchmark for embedding quality. Then the part that matters: thirty to fifty query-document pairs from YOUR data, where you KNOW the right answer; score each candidate by whether the correct doc lands in the top five. On cost: API models bill per token — trivial for most corpora; self-hosted via sentence-transformers gives privacy and no per-call cost, at the price of a GPU you now operate. Your Deloitte context likely means: API for prototypes, self-hosted when client data residency demands it.

scenes.title: Hindi + English? **Test it, don't assume it**
scenes.sub: Mixed-language corpora are the norm in India — and the failure mode
scenes.narration: Here's a scenario you know intimately: a corpus that's half English policies, half Hindi, with users asking in either language — sometimes mixed within one question. A model that's merely 'multilingual on paper' may cluster English well and Hindi poorly, or worse, never bridge the two — the Hindi policy and its English translation sitting in distant parts of the space. The test from GA-07's visualization chapter is exactly right here: embed known translation pairs, measure their similarity, and look at the plot. Cross-lingual pairs should hug. If they don't, that model is out — regardless of its benchmark average.

items.s: Embed 20 known EN↔HI pairs; median cosine should be high (0.7+)
Hindi query → must surface the English doc. Measure hit@5 per direction
Users write 'मुझे refund chahiye' — evaluate on REAL mixed queries

scenes.narration: The multilingual eval kit. One: translation pairs — same document in both languages should score high similarity; median below point seven is a red flag. Two: directional retrieval — Hindi query finding the English original, and the reverse; some models work one direction and fail the other. Three: code-switched queries — real users mix languages mid-sentence, and your eval should too, because a model that handles clean Hindi but chokes on Hinglish will fail in production. This thirty-minute test has saved more RAG projects than any architecture review.

scenes.title: Embedding is a **batch job** — price it like one
scenes.sub: Bulk discounts, Batch API, and the free tier nobody uses
scenes.narration: Good news: embedding is the cheap part of the pipeline. Text-embedding-3-small costs a tiny fraction of a cent per thousand tokens — a million typical documents usually land in the tens of dollars. Three optimizations: use the Batch API for initial backfills — the same roughly-half-price discount as the chat Batch API; batch requests — the embeddings endpoint accepts arrays of inputs up to thousands per call, which is also faster; and dimensionality reduction — OpenAI's models let you request fewer dimensions directly, cutting storage at a small quality cost. Embed once per document, store forever — reads are free.

items.s: input=[...1000 texts...] per call — fewer round trips, better throughput
avg 800 tokens/doc × 1M docs × price/1M = your backfill cost — usually small
Request reduced dimensions — Matryoshka truncation, ~⅓ storage for ~1-2% quality

scenes.narration: The levers. Batch your inputs — thousands of texts per request; the endpoint is built for it, and throughput improves dramatically. Do the multiplication once — average tokens per document times document count times price; for most corpora the number is smaller than a team lunch, which recalibrates how much optimization is worth. And if storage is the pressure, request reduced dimensions — OpenAI's models support Matryoshka truncation, where the first N dimensions preserve most of the quality. Cheaper storage, faster indexes, tiny quality cost — evaluate it on your golden pairs.

scenes.title: Changing models = **re-embedding everything**
scenes.sub: Dimensions change, geometry changes — there's no in-place upgrade
scenes.narration: The exit cost, stated plainly. Embedding models aren't interchangeable — different dimensionality, and even at equal dimensions, different geometry. A vector from model A means nothing to model B. Switching means: re-embed the entire corpus, rebuild every index, and re-run your retrieval evals. For a million documents this is hours of compute and a real bill. Sometimes it's worth it — a multilingual fix, a quality jump. But go in with eyes open: the cheapest embedding migration is the one you avoid by choosing well the first time.

items.s: Re-embedding requires the source — if you only kept vectors, you're stuck
Embed a sample with BOTH models; compare hit@5; cut over only when better
embed_model + embed_version per record — mixed-generation indexes are bugs

scenes.narration: The migration playbook. Always keep the source text — the vectors are derived, replaceable data; the text is the asset. Dual-run your eval set through both models before committing: new model wins on hit-at-five across your golden pairs, then cut over. And VERSION every vector with which model produced it — during migration you'll have two generations alive at once, and a query must only compare against its own generation. Architect's take: treat the embedding model like a database engine upgrade — planned, tested, reversible, and rare.

recap: Shortlist from MTEB, decide on YOUR 30-50 relevance pairs (hit@5)
Multilingual corpora need the translation-pair + cross-lingual + code-switch tests
Embedding is cheap: batch inputs, consider reduced dimensions; model switches = full re-embed — store source text and version every vector

quiz.q: Why run your own 30-50 relevance pairs instead of trusting the MTEB leaderboard?
opts: Leaderboards measure average quality on generic tasks; your pairs measure ranking quality on YOUR distribution
quiz.why: Domain text (legalese, code, Hinglish) behaves differently from benchmark averages. hit@5 on your own pairs is the decision metric.

quiz.q: You switch embedding models but keep the old vectors in the index. What breaks?
opts: Old and new vectors live in different geometries — comparisons are meaningless; you must re-embed and version
quiz.why: Different models = different spaces. Mixed-generation indexes silently return garbage rankings. Version vectors by model and re-embed fully on migration.

quiz.q: A corpus is 60% Hindi, 40% English. Which test best predicts production retrieval quality?
opts: Cross-lingual retrieval: Hindi queries must surface English docs and vice versa
quiz.why: Cross-lingual hit@5 in both directions is the direct measure — a model can excel monolingually yet place translation pairs far apart.

code.title: Embedding selection + backfill, done right
annot: Batch 1000 texts per call — throughput beats latency for backfills
hit@5 == 1.0 on your golden set is the bar; pay for 'large' only if 'small' misses
embed_model + version per record makes future migrations safe

notes:
# Embedding Models

## Choosing
- Shortlist: **MTEB leaderboard** → decide: your 30–50 query→doc pairs, score **hit@5**.
- API (OpenAI/Cohere/Voyage): zero ops. Self-hosted (sentence-transformers): privacy, GPU cost.

## Multilingual (EN + HI)
- Translation-pair test: EN↔HI pairs, median cosine ≥ ~0.7.
- Cross-lingual hit@5 BOTH directions.
- Code-switched queries ("मुझे refund chahiye") — evaluate on real mixed usage.

## Cost & batching
- Embedding is cheap: do the token math once (usually small $).
- Batch thousands of texts per call; Batch API for big backfills.
- `dimensions=512/1024` (Matryoshka) → ~⅓ storage for ~1-2% quality.
- Reads are free — embed once, store forever.

## Migration (re-embedding)
- Different model = different space → full re-embed, no in-place upgrade.
- **Store raw text** (the asset) + version every vector (embed_model, version).
- Dual-run eval on both models before cutover.
